case_data.title: Let's Talk AI: a people-centred approach to AI literacy
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
**Let’s Talk AI is a first-of-its-kind AI literacy campaign. It’s designed to bring conversations about artificial intelligence out of tech labs and boardrooms and move them onto our streets and into our homes. Through relatable cartoons and community stories, we’re breaking down the basics of AI in everyday life — whoever you are.**

From bus stops and community libraries, to radio waves and social media feeds, we made extensive efforts to appear across the communities we piloted in, to attempt to include as many people as possible. These comics are designed as a pilot for a national AI literacy campaign to encourage everyone to feel they can join conversations around AI in their lives. Three comics exist as the first phase, enabling people to reflect on how AI is changing people’s work and leisure, how we learn and how we look at the news and media.

We are inspired by a few things:
- Dr Susan Oman’s research – especially on the [Public Voices in AI project](https://digitalgood.net/dg-outputs/peoples-feelings-about-ai/)
- A wider movement to include all citizens in AI decision-making
- The belief that people deserve better understanding of AI in an AI-driven society
- The artwork of webtoon artist, Kitty McEwan
- The passion of Margaret Colling, a retired librarian from Morecambe Bay 
- The communities and experts we’ve spoken to along the way
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
**Resources**: 

Following action points from non-experts enables us to envisage doing things differently. It is a very powerful tool. However, it is very difficult in university, policy and research funding structures to find a way to resource exploratory work of this nature. Paying for offline marketing to raise awareness of the campaign in inclusive ways was the majority of the budget.  Paying artists fairly and participants fairly took the rest. 

This project was delivered through many gestures of good will by everyone else and this points to resource issues around doing things differently and doing them properly. The academic labour was unfunded and not resourced. This is not possible for most academics and should be recognised. 

**Accessibility:**

Making something universally accessible is not always possible. We had disagreements across the team on how to overcome issues. Accessibility advice on non-traditional outputs and presentation is not as well-established as for more typical products.
case_data.headline-findings:
AI literacy can be addressed through a general AI awareness-raising campaign, especially when it is designed to promote discussion through story-telling
A social-impact-focused AI awareness campaign demonstrated unexpected educational value for audiences who identified as being AI literate, despite the materials being designed for beginners.
case_data.participation-locations:
UK: Morecambe Bay and Lancaster; Sheffield; Plymouth. 
Some online groups took place with London-based participants at the trial stage and later stages.
case_data.additional-acknowledgements: This is not academic research in the strictest sense. It is instead the outcome of a call to action from the People’s Advisory Panel for the Public Voices in AI project that was coordinated by Connected By Data. Most specifically, it was executed as closely as possible to the vision of one specific participant, Margaret Colling, with the details co-produced through workshops in three locations and in collaboration with comic artist Kitty McEwan.
case_data.inclusion-efforts:
**Inclusion was prioritised across four dimensions:**

**Representation**: Diverse characters in the comics was an attempt to enable a broad range of people to identify with them.

**Geography**: Workshops took place in the three locations of the three core project team members: Susan (academic / lead, Sheffield); Margaret (public participant driving the project, Morecambe Bay and Lancaster); Kitty McEwan (artist / co-writer, Plymouth).

**Recruitment**: Snowball recruitment via community practitioners / organisations / infrastructure in the three locations, based on our networks.

**Accessibility**: Accessibility checks of materials in workshops and final products.
case_data.project-title: Let's Talk AI: a people-centred approach to AI literacy
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
It is the first, as far as we know, AI Awareness campaign that has been devised by 'the people', then designed with 'the people' in order to create AI literacy that serves 'the people'. 
It directly responds to a prior call to action from participants: taking public voice seriously to change practice with a view to impact.
The innovative webtoon format has not been used in research before, and it is the first national AI literacy campaign to utilise a combination of broadcast and paid online and offline marketing to raise awareness.
The project has been on BBC news online, the BBC came to film some of the team. We've been on local radio, in parliament and in the Guardian. 
The project was chosen as part of the official UK delegation to the India AI Impact summit, organised by the British Council and the UK's Foreign office. Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy featured it on his social media highlights, as did local Delhi residents and the British Council's Alison Barrett MBE.

data.additional-notes: Resources restricted the number of participants, as we wanted three touch points for people to shape the whole campaign: its materials and messaging, from start to finish. We were aiming for breadth of ethnicity, faith, age, class and other proxy demographics, but only to gain input from a variety of places. This was never conceived as being exhaustive, nor was it able to be perfect in terms of participatory methods
data.recruitment-description: The 3 core project members are based in the 3 locations: Morecambe Bay / Lancaster; Sheffield; Plymouth. We used our own networks to approach community organisations and / or leaders to help us organise workshop spaces and recruit participants.
data.was-there-a-specific-target-population: We wanted a spread of communities in the 3 locations, rather than a specific targeted demographic
